first_impression: Gorgeous deck, clear spine, honest numbers. But who pays? No users, no revenue, niche audience of RL classes.
confusing: Slide 6 '3.2 days of practice' is simulated robot time; a non-expert hears wall-clock and the headline overclaims
Slide 13 market is 'RL classes on MacBooks' with zero users and no named course or teacher
Slide 12 admits agents wrote most of the code; unclear what the 16-year-old actually built vs directed
Slides 9 and 10 are dense with numbers for a 3-minute pitch
doubts: 'Same answers as the pro simulator' headline vs the chart where passive collapse diverges visibly and the walker only agrees for 0.6-0.8 s
40x is vs a CPU path on a simpler 2D engine; the headline hides that in small print
DVHS club and own hackathons count as 'first users', but none have used it yet
Hosted classroom and edu licenses is a slide-footer afterthought, not a business model
questions: Name one teacher or club that has committed to using this, and when?
Why would a class pick MacGym over free Colab when RL courses already run on Gymnasium and CPU MuJoCo?
What do you personally own in the code if agents wrote most of it?
What is the one thing you would build next week if you won?

fixes.change: Replace the generic audience with one concrete commitment: a named club or class, a date for the workshop, and a number of students reached or signed up
Retitle to 'Matches MuJoCo on textbook physics; contact diverges after 0.8 s' so the headline matches the evidence
Label the headline 'simulated robot time' in the big type, not only in the eyebrow
Lead with what you built and decided; move the agent disclosure to a one-liner and show a diff or code stat for your own contribution
Cut slide 12 or slide 9 to keep the pitch inside 3 minutes and give the live demo more time

first_impression: Metal kernel codegen plus a MuJoCo CPU baseline, and he admits it's 2D. More honest than most. Still not MJX or Warp.
confusing: Slide 2 'GPU idle' framing: MJX and Warp comparisons are waved away as NVIDIA-only, with no CPU MJX number
Slide 10 40x is against MuJoCo C rollout on CPU, a weak baseline for a GPU claim; the apples-to-apples GPU comparison is absent
Slide 5 metal excerpt is truncated and shows only the motor, not contacts or the solver
doubts: Planar 2D with 7 capsules and ground-only impulse contacts is a very small physics workload; 6.8M steps/s says little about real robot sim
Sim-to-sim to MuJoCo is the same author's model in both, so transfer proves little; mass +20% already gives 3/20 falls
Full 'about 3.7x from GPU alone' is a mild number, and PPO is 72% of time, so the Metal kernel win barely matters for end-to-end training
'jax-metal consider it dead' is a single quote used to sweep the whole Apple GPU ecosystem aside
questions: What is steps/s for MJX on the same M3 CPU, and for Warp on any NVIDIA GPU, same walker?
How many contacts per body and what solver precision; is it float32 with Gauss-Seidel iterations?
If PPO update is 72% of an iteration, what is end-to-end speedup versus CPU MuJoCo plus the same MLX PPO?
Does the kernel scale past 7 bodies, or does one-thread-per-robot collapse on larger articulated robots?

fixes.change: Add an end-to-end bar: time to 10 m walking, MacGym vs MuJoCo CPU rollout plus the same PPO, so the number reflects training not raw physics
Show the full contact and solver section of the generated Metal kernel with line counts and threadgroup config
State the MJX-on-CPU number or an explicit 'not run' on the slide, not only in notes
Add one sim-to-sim row with a model that differs from the training sim (changed solver or contact params) to make transfer meaningful
Cut the jax-metal quote and replace with a measured line: what Mac users actually do today and how long it takes
